gancho: Antes de zarpar, em 1628, o navio de guerra sueco Vasa passou por um teste: trinta homens correram de um lado a outro do convés. O almirante parou tudo, com medo de que ele virasse. O navio partiu e afundou.
explicacao: O Vasa afundou na viagem inaugural, em 10 de agosto de 1628, depois de navegar cerca de 1.300 metros, diante de uma multidão de moradores de Estocolmo. No verão daquele ano, o capitão encarregado da obra tinha organizado uma demonstração para o vice-almirante Fleming: trinta homens correram de um bordo ao outro para fazer o casco balançar, e o almirante mandou parar depois de só três travessias. O rei Gustavo Adolfo, porém, mandava cartas e mais cartas pedindo que o navio fosse logo para o mar. No dia da partida, uma rajada mais forte deitou o casco até as portinholas abertas dos canhões ficarem abaixo da água. O defeito era de projeto: a parte acima da linha d'água era alta e pesada demais em relação à que ficava submersa. Foram achadas ainda quatro réguas usadas pelos operários: duas em pés suecos, de 12 polegadas, e duas em pés de Amsterdã, de 11. O casco também é assimétrico, com mais peso a bombordo, e uma explicação provável é que equipes diferentes trabalharam com réguas diferentes. Mas o que derrubou o navio foi o excesso de peso no alto. No inquérito, ninguém foi punido: o rei havia aprovado as medidas, e a culpa acabou caindo sobre o construtor original, que já tinha morrido.

fontes.trecho: The ship sank after sailing roughly 1,300 m (1,400 yd) into her maiden voyage on 10 August 1628. [...] In the summer of 1628, the captain responsible for supervising construction of the ship, Söfring Hansson, arranged for the ship's stability to be demonstrated for Vice Admiral Fleming, who had recently arrived in Stockholm from Prussia. Thirty men ran back and forth across the upper deck to start the ship rolling, but the admiral stopped the test after they had made only three trips, as he feared the ship would capsize. [...] Gustavus Adolphus had been sending a steady stream of letters insisting that the ship be put to sea as soon as possible. [...] At Tegelviken, where there is a gap in the bluffs, an even stronger gust again forced the ship onto her port side, this time pushing the open lower gunports under the surface, allowing water to rush in onto the lower gundeck. [...] Vasa sank in full view of a crowd of hundreds, if not thousands, of mostly ordinary Stockholmers who had come to see the ship set sail. [...] In the end, no one was punished or found guilty for negligence, and the blame effectively fell on the dead Henrik Hybertsson. [...] Gustavus Adolphus had approved all measurements and armaments [...] The part of the hull above the waterline was too high and too heavily built in relation to the amount of hull in the water. [...] Four rulers used by the workmen who built the ship have been found; two were calibrated in Swedish feet, of 12 Swedish inches, and the other two were calibrated in Amsterdam feet, of 11 Amsterdam inches. The use of different units of length on the two sides of the vessel caused the ship to be heavier on the port side.

gancho: Em 1919, um tanque de melaço estourou em Boston e uma onda de melaço matou 21 pessoas. Ele vazava tanto que tinha sido pintado de marrom para disfarçar, e moradores recolhiam o melaço que escorria.
explicacao: O tanque tinha 15 metros de altura e guardava até 8.700 metros cúbicos de melaço, matéria-prima de etanol. Em 15 de janeiro de 1919, ele se rompeu e soltou pelas ruas do bairro North End uma onda de até 8 metros, a uma velocidade estimada em 56 km/h. Um inquérito mostrou que o tesoureiro da empresa, que acompanhou a obra sem nenhuma experiência em engenharia, dispensou testes básicos, como encher o tanque com água para procurar vazamentos, e não deu atenção aos rangidos que ele soltava a cada enchimento. Uma análise de 2014, com métodos modernos, concluiu que o aço tinha metade da espessura devida mesmo pelos padrões da época e era mais quebradiço por falta de manganês. A física do melaço agravou a tragédia. Na véspera, uma carga aquecida para fluir melhor tinha sido posta no tanque. Segundo um estudo de Harvard de 2016, o líquido correu depressa no começo, mas esfriou ao se espalhar no inverno e ficou muito mais espesso, prendendo as vítimas. O processo coletivo movido por 119 moradores é considerado um marco na regulação das empresas.

fontes.trecho: The Great Molasses Flood, also known as the Boston Molasses Disaster, was a disaster that occurred on January 15, 1919, in the North End neighborhood of Boston, Massachusetts. A large storage tank filled with 2.3 million U.S. gallons (8,700 cubic meters) of molasses, weighing approximately 13,000 short tons (12,000 metric tons) burst, and the resultant wave of molasses rushed through the streets at an estimated 35 miles per hour (56 kilometers per hour), killing 21 and injuring 150 people. [...] Molasses can be fermented to produce ethanol [...] The molasses tank stood 50 feet (15 meters) tall and 90 ft (27 m) in diameter, and contained as much as 2.3 million US gal (8,700 m3). [...] On the previous day, a ship had delivered a fresh load of molasses, which had been warmed to decrease its viscosity for transfer. [...] The collapse translated this energy into a wave of molasses 25 ft (8 m) high at its peak, moving at 35 mph (56 km/h). [...] In the wake of the accident, 119 residents brought a class-action lawsuit against the United States Industrial Alcohol Company (USIA) [...] is considered a milestone in the development of modern corporate regulation. [...] An inquiry after the disaster revealed that Arthur Jell, USIA's treasurer, neglected basic safety tests while overseeing construction of the tank, such as filling it with water insufficient to check for leaks, and ignored warning signs such as groaning noises each time the tank was filled. He had no architectural or engineering experience. When filled with molasses, the tank leaked so badly that it was painted brown to hide the leakage. Local residents collected leaked molasses for their homes. A 2014 investigation applied modern engineering analysis and found that the steel was half as thick as it should have been for a tank of its size even with the lower standards of the time. Another issue was that the steel lacked manganese, and was more brittle as a result. [...] In 2016, a team of scientists and students at Harvard University conducted extensive studies of the disaster [...] The Harvard study concluded that the molasses cooled and thickened quickly as it rushed through the streets, hampering efforts to free victims before they suffocated.

gancho: Em 1981, duas passarelas de um hotel nos EUA desabaram e mataram 114 pessoas. Uma mudança para facilitar a montagem, que parecia inofensiva, fez as vigas de cima segurarem também a passarela de baixo.
explicacao: No Hyatt Regency de Kansas City, a passarela do quarto andar ficava logo acima da do segundo. No projeto original, barras de aço desciam do teto, atravessavam as vigas do quarto andar e seguravam também a passarela de baixo. Assim, as vigas de cima só carregavam o próprio piso. O fabricante das barras notou que, desse jeito, a barra teria de ser toda rosqueada abaixo do quarto andar, e as roscas podiam se estragar na montagem. Propôs então dois conjuntos separados: um pendurando o quarto andar no teto e outro pendurando o segundo andar no quarto. Parece equivalente, mas não é: as vigas do quarto andar passaram a sustentar as duas passarelas e só aguentavam 30% dessa carga. O projeto original, aliás, já ficava em 60% do mínimo exigido pelo código de obras da cidade. Na noite de 17 de julho, cerca de 1.600 pessoas estavam no saguão para um chá dançante. Os investigadores concluíram que as passarelas cairiam com um terço do peso que tinham naquela noite. A empresa de engenharia perdeu as licenças em vários estados americanos, e o engenheiro responsável acabou assumindo a culpa e virou palestrante sobre desastres. O caso se tornou lição de ética e segurança na engenharia.

fontes.trecho: On July 17, 1981, two overhead walkways in the Hyatt Regency Hotel in Kansas City, Missouri, collapsed, killing 114 people and injuring 216. [...] An investigation concluded that it would have failed under one-third of the weight it held that night. Convicted of gross negligence, misconduct and unprofessional conduct, the engineering company lost its national affiliation and all engineering licenses in four states, but was acquitted of criminal charges. Company owner and engineer of record Jack D. Gillum eventually claimed full responsibility for the collapse and its unchecked design flaws, and he became an engineering disaster lecturer. The disaster contributed many lessons and reforms to engineering ethics and safety [...] The fourth-level walkway was directly above the second-level walkway. [...] About 1,600 people gathered in the Kansas City hotel's atrium for such a dance on the evening of Friday, July 17, 1981. [...] This original design supported 60% of the minimum load required by Kansas City building codes. Havens Steel Company had manufactured the rods, and the company noted that the whole rod below the fourth floor would have to be threaded in order to screw on the nuts to hold the fourth-floor walkway in place. These threads would be subject to damage as the fourth-floor structure was hoisted into place. Havens Steel proposed that two separate and offset sets of rods be used: the first set suspending the fourth-floor walkway from the ceiling, and the second set suspending the second-floor walkway from the fourth-floor walkway. This design change would be fatal. In the original design, the beams of the fourth-floor walkway had to support the weight of the fourth-floor walkway, with the weight of the second-floor walkway supported completely by the rods. In the revised design, however, the fourth-floor beams supported both the fourth- and second-floor walkways, but were only strong enough for 30% of that load.

gancho: A ponte do Milênio, em Londres, fechou dois dias após abrir, em 2000, porque balançava de lado. A explicação clássica: os pedestres entravam no ritmo do balanço sem perceber e o reforçavam. Hoje isso é questionado.
explicacao: A passarela sobre o Tâmisa foi aberta em 10 de junho de 2000 e recebeu 90 mil pessoas no primeiro dia, com até 2 mil sobre ela ao mesmo tempo. O fenômeno era então pouco estudado. O balanço natural de quem anda empurrava a ponte um pouco para os lados; quando o piso se deslocava, cada pessoa se ajustava para não cair, e todas faziam isso ao mesmo tempo. Isso reforçava a oscilação, que por sua vez sincronizava ainda mais os passos, num ciclo de realimentação positiva. O balanço máximo chegou a uns 70 milímetros. O risco vertical já era conhecido: é por isso que tropas quebram o passo ao atravessar pontes, e a Albert Bridge, também em Londres, tem uma placa de 1873 pedindo isso aos soldados. A Arup, que projetou a ponte, estudou o efeito e o chamou de excitação lateral síncrona. Enrijecer a estrutura mudaria demais a aparência, então a solução foi instalar 37 amortecedores viscosos e 52 amortecedores de massa sintonizada, ao custo de 5 milhões de libras. Um estudo publicado em 2021 na Nature Communications contestou essa versão: para os autores, os passos coordenados foram consequência do balanço, e não a causa, porque o jeito como cada pedestre se equilibra já bastaria para alimentar a oscilação, mesmo sem sincronia. A ponte reabriu em fevereiro de 2002 e não voltou a balançar, mas o apelido de "ponte bamba" ficou.

fontes.trecho: The bridge opened on 10 June 2000, one month late. Unexpected lateral vibration due to resonant structural response caused the bridge to be closed on 12 June for modifications. [...] The vibration was attributed to a then under-researched phenomenon whereby pedestrians crossing a bridge that has a lateral sway have an unconscious tendency to match their footsteps to the sway, exacerbating it. This is different from the well-understood problem of vertical sway, which is why troops stop marching in stride together as a unit when crossing such a bridge. An example is London's Albert Bridge, which has a sign dating from 1873 warning marching ranks of soldiers to break step while crossing. [...] The bridge's movements were caused by a positive feedback phenomenon, known as synchronous lateral excitation. The natural sway motion of people walking caused small sideways oscillations in the bridge, which in turn caused people on the bridge to sway in step, increasing the amplitude of the bridge oscillations and continually reinforcing the effect; the maximum sway was around 70 millimetres (2.8 in). On the day of opening, the bridge was crossed by 90,000 people, with up to 2,000 on the bridge at a time. [...] When the bridge lurches to one side, the pedestrians must adjust to keep from falling over, and they all do this at the same time. [...] Engineers at Arup, the company that designed the bridge, conducted research into the unexpected oscillation, which they called 'synchronous lateral excitation'. [...] They concluded that making the bridge stiffer, to move its resonant frequency out of the excitation range, was not feasible as it would greatly change its appearance. Instead, the resonance was controlled by retrofitting 37 viscous fluid dampers to dissipate energy. [...] Additionally, 52 tuned mass dampers add inertia to control vertical movement. The work took from May 2001 to January 2002 and cost £5 million. After a period of testing, the bridge was reopened on 22 February 2002 and, since that date, has not been subject to significant vibration. In spite of the successful cure, the "wobbly bridge" (sometimes "wibbly-wobbly") epithet remains in common usage among Londoners.

fontes.titulo: Emergence of the London Millennium Bridge instability without synchronisation (Nature Communications, 2021)
fontes.trecho: Published: 10 December 2021 [...] The pedestrian-induced instability of the London Millennium Bridge is a widely used example of Kuramoto synchronisation. Yet, reviewing observational, experimental, and modelling evidence, we argue that increased coherence of pedestrians’ foot placement is a consequence of, not a cause of the instability. Instead, uncorrelated pedestrians produce positive feedback, through negative damping on average, that can initiate significant lateral bridge vibration over a wide range of natural frequencies.

gancho: Em 1996, o primeiro Ariane 5 saiu da rota 37 segundos após decolar e se destruiu por um erro num cálculo que não servia para nada depois da decolagem. Os dois sistemas de navegação, um reserva do outro, pararam juntos.
explicacao: O foguete europeu reaproveitou o software do sistema de referência inercial do Ariane 4. Uma função de alinhamento continuava rodando por uns 40 segundos de voo, exigência do modelo antigo que, no Ariane 5, já não tinha utilidade depois da decolagem. Como o novo foguete ganhava velocidade horizontal maior no começo do voo, um valor calculado ficou grande demais na conversão de um número de 64 bits para um inteiro de 16 bits, e o resultado estourou. Para poupar o processador, os programadores tinham protegido só quatro de sete variáveis críticas, com base em faixas de valores que valiam para a trajetória do Ariane 4. A especificação mandava parar o processador diante de qualquer exceção. Como os dois módulos rodavam o mesmo software, os dois pararam, e o padrão de bits do diagnóstico foi lido como dado de voo. O relatório da comissão de inquérito criticou a visão de que o software deve ser tido como correto até que se prove o contrário e registrou que a função nunca foi testada com dados da trajetória do Ariane 5. O prejuízo passou de 370 milhões de dólares, e o caso deu impulso à pesquisa sobre a confiabilidade de sistemas críticos.

fontes.trecho: Ariane flight V88, also known as Ariane 5 Flight 501, was the failed maiden flight of the Arianespace Ariane 5 rocket, vehicle no. 501, on 4 June 1996. [...] This caused the rocket to veer off its flight path 37 seconds after launch, beginning to disintegrate under high aerodynamic forces, and finally self-destructing via its automated flight termination system. [...] The failure resulted in a loss of more than US$370 million. [...] The Ariane 5 reused the code from the inertial reference platform from the Ariane 4, but the early part of the Ariane 5's flight path differed from the Ariane 4 in having higher horizontal velocity values. [...] The alignment function was operative for approximately 40 seconds of flight, which was based on a requirement of Ariane 4, but served no purpose after lift-off on the Ariane 5. The greater values of BH caused a data conversion from a 64-bit floating point number to a 16-bit signed integer value to overflow and cause a hardware exception. The programmers had protected only four out of seven critical variables against overflow to keep within a required maximum workload target of 80% for the on-board Inertial Reference System computer, and relied on assumptions which were correct for the trajectory of Ariane 4, but not Ariane 5, regarding the possible range of values for the three unprotected variables. The exception halted both of the inertial reference system modules, although they were intended to be redundant. The active module presented a diagnostic bit pattern to the On-Board Computer which was interpreted as flight data [...] which stipulated that in the event of any detected exception the processor was to be stopped. [...] the view had been taken that software should be considered correct until it is shown to be at fault. [...] the loss of a proper software function is hazardous because the same software runs in both SRI units. [...] Consequently, the realignment function was not tested under simulated Ariane 5 flight conditions, and the design error was not discovered. [...] resulting in increased support for research on ensuring the reliability of safety-critical systems.

gancho: Entre 1985 e 1987, uma máquina de radioterapia causou overdoses de radiação, algumas fatais. O fabricante garantia que era impossível e não reproduzia a falha; um físico de hospital insistiu até reproduzi-la.
explicacao: O Therac-25, do fabricante canadense AECL, chegou ao mercado no fim de 1982. Nos modelos anteriores, travas físicas impediam certas falhas; no novo, elas foram retiradas e trocadas por verificações feitas pelo software, que reaproveitava código das máquinas antigas. Entre 1985 e 1987 houve pelo menos seis acidentes com doses muito acima do previsto, e três dos pacientes atingidos morreram em consequência. Várias mensagens de erro diziam só "MALFUNCTION" seguido de um número, e funcionários do fabricante garantiam aos operadores que uma overdose era impossível, o que os levava a descartar a máquina como causa. Em um dos casos, a equipe atribuiu os sintomas ao próprio câncer da paciente. Depois de um acidente num hospital do Texas, o físico do hospital e a operadora trabalharam duro até descobrir que a rapidez na edição dos dados era decisiva para o erro aparecer. O fabricante dizia não conseguir reproduzi-lo e só conseguiu seguindo as instruções do físico. Os investigadores apontaram ainda que o software não passou por revisão independente e que a combinação de programa e equipamento nunca tinha sido testada antes da montagem no hospital. O caso virou estudo de caso em engenharia de software e ética na computação, como exemplo do excesso de confiança de engenheiros que desprezam os relatos de quem usa a máquina.

fontes.trecho: The Therac-25 was involved in at least six incident overdoses of radiation between 1985 and 1987 [...] The Therac-25 has become a case study in health informatics, software engineering, and computer ethics. The incidents highlight the dangers of engineer overconfidence after the engineers dismissed end user reports, leading to severe consequences. [...] AECL decided not to duplicate some safety mechanisms, and reused modules and code routines from the Therac-20 for the Therac-25. The first prototype of the Therac-25 was built in 1976 and was put on the market in late 1982. [...] Previous models had hardware interlocks to prevent such faults, but the Therac-25 had removed them, depending instead on software checks for safety. [...] in three cases, the injured patients later died as a result of the overdose. [...] The staff at the treatment center did not believe it was possible for the Therac-25 to cause such an injury, and it was treated as a symptom of her cancer. [...] === East Texas Cancer Center, Tyler, March 1986 === [...] After strenuous work, the physicist and operator were able to reproduce the error 54 message. They determined that speed in editing the data entry was a key factor in producing error 54. [...] AECL stated they could not reproduce the error and they only got it after following the instructions of the physicist so that the data entry was very rapid. [...] The software was not reviewed independently. [...] Machine operators were reassured by AECL personnel that overdoses were impossible, leading them to dismiss the Therac-25 as the potential cause of many incidents. The Therac-25 had never been tested with the combination of software and hardware until it was assembled at the hospital. [...] Several error messages merely displayed the word "MALFUNCTION" followed by a number from 1 to 64.

gancho: A ilha artificial do aeroporto de Kansai, no Japão, afundou 8,2 m até 1999, quase 50% além da previsão mais otimista. O terminal se apoia em colunas que são alongadas pondo chapas de metal na base.
explicacao: O antigo aeroporto de Osaka não tinha como crescer e incomodava os vizinhos com o barulho, então o novo foi construído numa ilha no meio da baía. Ali há 18 metros de água sobre 20 metros de argila mole, que é 70% água. Antes de aterrar, os engenheiros cravaram um milhão de drenos de areia para tirar água da argila e endurecê-la. Três montanhas foram escavadas para fornecer a terra da primeira ilha. O peso do aterro comprimiu o fundo do mar, como já se esperava, mas mais do que o previsto: a estimativa mais otimista era de 5,7 metros, e em 1999 a ilha já tinha baixado 8,2. Para compensar o afundamento, o terminal, cuja construção começou em 1991, foi projetado sobre colunas ajustáveis, que são estendidas com a inserção de chapas grossas de metal na base. O ritmo de afundamento caiu de 50 centímetros por ano em 1994 para 7 em 2008. A obra resistiu bem a outros testes: no terremoto de 1995, com epicentro a cerca de 20 km, juntas deslizantes protegeram o aeroporto, e nem os vidros quebraram. As lições foram usadas em outras ilhas-aeroporto, como as de Kobe e de Hong Kong.

fontes.trecho: The city's original international airport, Itami Airport, located in the densely populated suburbs of Itami and Toyonaka, was surrounded by buildings; it could not be expanded, and many of its neighbours had filed complaints because of noise pollution problems. [...] It is located on the artificial island of Kankūjima (関空島), in the middle of Osaka Bay [...] The water depth is 18 metres (59 ft) on top of 20 metres (66 ft) of soft Holocene clay which holds 70% water. A million sand drains were built into the clay to remove water and solidify the clay. [...] Three mountains were excavated for 21 million cubic metres (27 million cubic yards), and 180 million cubic metres (240 million cubic yards) was used to construct island 1. [...] The island had been predicted to sink 5.7 m (18 ft 8 in) by the most optimistic estimate as the weight of the material used for construction compressed the seabed silts. However, by 1999, the island had sunk 8.2 m (26 ft 11 in) – almost 50% more than predicted. [...] Much of what was learned went into the successful artificial islands in silt deposits for New Kitakyushu Airport, Kobe Airport, and Chubu Centrair International Airport. The lessons of Kansai Airport were also applied in the construction of Hong Kong International Airport. In 1991, the terminal construction commenced. To compensate for the sinking of the island, adjustable columns were designed to support the terminal building. These are extended by inserting thick metal plates at their bases. [...] On 17 January 1995, Japan was struck by the Great Hanshin earthquake, the epicenter of which was about 20 km (12 mi) away from KIX [...] Its earthquake engineering, particularly the use of sliding joints, allowed the airport to emerge unscathed. Even the glass in the windows remained intact. [...] Most additional costs were initially due to the island's sinking, caused by the soft soils of Osaka Bay, which was anticipated by designers. The sink rate fell from 50 cm (20 in) per year during 1994 to 7 cm (3 in) per year in 2008.

gancho: O "bug do milênio" quase não causou estragos, e ainda se discute por quê. Céticos citam Coreia do Sul, Itália e Rússia, que teriam gastado pouco e não tiveram mais problemas que quem gastou fortunas.
explicacao: Muitos programas guardavam o ano só com os dois últimos dígitos, e 2000 ficaria igual a 1900. Bob Bemer percebeu o risco em 1958 e passou vinte anos tentando, sem sucesso, chamar a atenção de programadores, da IBM e do governo dos EUA. O custo total da preparação provavelmente passou de 300 bilhões de dólares. Na virada, houve falhas pequenas e curiosas: em Oslo, uma creche ofereceu vaga a uma senhora de 105 anos, e uma locadora sul-coreana cobrou uma multa de cerca de 7 mil dólares por uma fita "atrasada" 100 anos. Os dois lados ainda discordam. Os céticos lembram que escolas e pequenas empresas que fizeram pouco ou nada quase não tiveram problemas, e dizem que a escala do risco foi muito superestimada. Os defensores respondem que muitas correções chegaram anos antes, embutidas em atualizações de rotina, e que grandes empresas e governos raramente divulgaram o que evitaram. O presidente Bill Clinton chamou o caso de "o primeiro desafio do século XXI vencido com sucesso".

fontes.trecho: Many programs represented four-digit years with only the final two digits, e.g. 1985 as 85, making the year 2000 indistinguishable from 1900. [...] U.S. President Bill Clinton, who organized efforts to minimize the damage in the United States, labelled Y2K as "the first challenge of the 21st century successfully met" [...] The first person known to publicly address this issue was Bob Bemer, who had noticed it in 1958 as a result of work on genealogical software. He spent the next twenty years fruitlessly trying to raise awareness of the problem with programmers, IBM, the government of the United States and the International Organization for Standardization. [...] In Norway, a day care center for kindergarteners in Oslo offered a spot to a 105-year-old woman because the citizen's registry only showed the last two digits of citizens' years of birth. [...] a video store in Gwangju accidentally generated a late fee of approximately 8 million won (approximately $7,000 US dollars) because the store's computer determined a tape rental to be 100 years overdue. [...] The total cost of the work done in preparation for Y2K likely surpassed US$300 billion [...] Expected problems that were not seen by small businesses and small organizations were prevented by Y2K fixes embedded in routine updates to operating system and utility software that were applied several years before 31 December 1999. The extent to which larger industry and government fixes averted issues that would have more significant impacts had they not been fixed were typically not disclosed or widely reported. [...] and that the scale of the problem had therefore been severely overestimated. Countries such as South Korea, Italy, and Russia invested little to nothing in Y2K remediation, yet had the same negligible Y2K problems as countries that spent enormous sums of money. [...] Critics also cite the lack of Y2K-related problems in schools, many of which undertook little or no remediation effort. [...] Similarly, there were few Y2K-related problems in an estimated 1.5 million small businesses that undertook no remediation effort.

gancho: A sonda Mars Climate Orbiter se perdeu em 1999 porque um programa dava o impulso em libras-força e outro lia em newtons. Ao menos dois navegadores notaram o desvio antes, mas foram ignorados por causa de um formulário.
explicacao: Lançada pela NASA em dezembro de 1998, a sonda deveria entrar em órbita de Marte a cerca de 226 km de altitude. Um software de solo da Lockheed Martin, que construiu a sonda, calculava o impulso dos propulsores em libras-força vezes segundo, contrariando a especificação combinada. O programa de trajetória da NASA tratava esses números como newtons-segundo, uma diferença de 4,45 vezes, e usava o resultado para atualizar a posição prevista da nave. Na semana anterior à chegada, a equipe de navegação viu que a altitude de inserção podia ser bem menor que a planejada; um dia antes, as contas já indicavam 110 km, perto dos 80 km que se considerava o mínimo suportável. Pelo menos dois navegadores tinham notado a discrepância, mas suas preocupações foram descartadas porque eles "não seguiram as regras" de preenchimento do formulário de registro. Uma manobra de correção estava no cronograma e chegou a ser combinada numa reunião, mas não foi feita. Cálculos posteriores mostraram que a trajetória passaria a 57 km da superfície. A NASA não jogou a culpa na empresa: seus próprios dirigentes disseram que a agência falhou ao não fazer as checagens e os testes que teriam pegado o erro.

fontes.trecho: The Mars Climate Orbiter (formerly the Mars Surveyor '98 Orbiter) was a robotic space probe launched by NASA on December 11, 1998 [...] It was intended to place the spacecraft at an optimal position for an orbital insertion maneuver that would bring the spacecraft around Mars at an altitude of 226 km (140 mi) on September 23, 1999. However, during the week between TCM-4 and the orbital insertion maneuver, the navigation team reported that it appeared the insertion altitude could be much lower than planned, at about 150–170 km (93–106 mi). Twenty-four hours prior to orbital insertion, calculations placed the orbiter at an altitude of 110 km (68 mi). 80 km (50 mi) was the minimum altitude that Mars Climate Orbiter was thought to be capable of surviving during this maneuver. [...] post-failure calculations showed that the spacecraft's trajectory would have taken it within 57 km (35 mi) of the surface. [...] The primary cause of this discrepancy was that one piece of ground software supplied by Lockheed Martin produced results in a United States customary unit, contrary to its Software Interface Specification (SIS), while a second system, supplied by NASA, expected those results to be in SI units, in accordance with the SIS. Specifically, software that calculated the total impulse produced by thruster firings produced results in pound-force seconds. The trajectory calculation software then used these results – expected to be in newton-seconds (incorrect by a factor of 4.45) – to update the predicted position of the spacecraft. Still, NASA does not place the responsibility on Lockheed for the mission loss; instead, various officials at NASA have stated that NASA itself was at fault for failing to make the appropriate checks and tests that would have caught the discrepancy. The discrepancy between calculated and measured position, resulting in the discrepancy between desired and actual orbit insertion altitude, had been noticed earlier by at least two navigators, whose concerns were dismissed because they "did not follow the rules about filling out [the] form to document their concerns". [...] Attendees of the meeting recall an agreement to conduct TCM-5, but it was ultimately not done.

gancho: Na Segunda Guerra, alguns cargueiros dos EUA se partiram ao meio sem aviso. Uma metalurgista de Cambridge mostrou que o culpado não era a solda malfeita, e sim o aço, que fica frágil abaixo de certa temperatura.
explicacao: Os navios Liberty foram os primeiros cargueiros pré-fabricados totalmente soldados, e os EUA construíram 2.710 deles. Durante a guerra houve quase 1.500 casos de fratura frágil importantes, e doze navios, entre eles três Liberty, partiram-se ao meio. A suspeita caiu sobre os estaleiros, que usavam operários inexperientes e técnicas novas de solda para produzir depressa. Constance Tipper mostrou que as trincas não nasciam nas soldas: abaixo de uma temperatura crítica, aquele aço deixava de ser dúctil e virava frágil, e o Atlântico Norte chegava a essas temperaturas. A solda pesava de outro jeito. Num casco rebitado, a trinca parava na borda de cada chapa; no casco soldado, praticamente uma folha contínua de aço, ela corria livre. Cantos quadrados de escotilhas sobre costuras de solda concentravam a tensão. Tipper criou um ensaio, hoje chamado teste Tipper, para conferir o metal dos navios. Ela já tinha recebido, em 1923, a Medalha Bakeriana da Royal Society com G. I. Taylor, mas foi barrada do jantar da premiação por ser mulher. Mais tarde, foi a única mulher em tempo integral no corpo docente de engenharia de Cambridge.

fontes.trecho: During World War II there were nearly 1,500 instances of significant brittle fractures. Twelve ships, including three of the 2,710 Liberty ships built, broke in half without warning [...] Suspicion fell on the shipyards, which had often used inexperienced workers and new welding techniques to produce large numbers of ships in great haste. [...] Constance Tipper of Cambridge University demonstrated that the fractures did not start in the welds, but were due to the embrittlement of the steel used. When used in riveted construction, however, the same steel did not have this problem. [...] Ships in the North Atlantic were exposed to temperatures that could fall below this critical point. The predominantly welded hull construction, effectively a continuous sheet of steel, allowed small cracks to propagate unimpeded, unlike in a hull made of separate plates riveted together. One common type of crack nucleated at the square corner of a hatch which coincided with a welded seam, both the corner and the weld acting as stress concentrators.

She investigated brittle fracture and the ductile-brittle transition of metals used in the construction of warships, and was the first female full-time faculty member at Cambridge University Department of Engineering. [...] In 1923, under the name C. F. Elam she received the Royal Society's Bakerian Medal with G. I. Taylor. Unfortunately, the Royal Society had not realized that she was a woman and their dinner club did not allow women attendees. [...] In 1949 Tipper was appointed as a reader at Cambridge University, becoming the only full-time woman member of the faculty of engineering. [...] These ships were built in the US between 1941 and 1945, and were the first all-welded pre-fabricated cargo ships. Tipper established that the fractures were not caused by welding, but were due to the properties of the steel itself. She demonstrated that there is a critical temperature below which the fracture mode in steel changes from ductile to brittle. [...] She developed what is now known as the "Tipper Test" to help ensure that the metal used in ship construction was sufficiently sound.

gancho: Muitos engenheiros canadenses usam no mindinho um anel de ferro que lembra suas obrigações. Diz o mito que os primeiros saíram das vigas da ponte de Quebec, que desabou em 1907. Mas foram feitos por veteranos de guerra.
explicacao: A ponte de Quebec, sobre o rio São Lourenço, falhou duas vezes durante a obra, em 1907 e em 1916, e as duas quedas custaram 88 vidas. Na primeira, a equipe no canteiro percebeu que peças já instaladas estavam se deformando: a estrutura pesava muito mais do que aguentava, porque cálculos preliminares nunca tinham sido conferidos. O engenheiro do local escreveu várias vezes ao engenheiro consultor, Theodore Cooper, que de início respondeu que os problemas eram pequenos. Quando Cooper finalmente mandou parar de pôr carga na ponte, o aviso não chegou a tempo, e um braço da estrutura caiu no rio em 15 segundos, matando 75 dos 86 operários; 33 deles (algumas fontes dizem 35) eram metalúrgicos mohawks de Kahnawake. Em 1922, o professor H. E. T. Haultain propôs um juramento ético para engenheiros, e o texto da cerimônia foi escrito por Rudyard Kipling. O anel, de faces ásperas, é usado no dedo mínimo da mão com que se escreve, para raspar no papel e servir de lembrete. Hoje, fora de Toronto, os anéis são de aço inoxidável. A história de que o ferro veio da ponte caída é um mito persistente: o primeiro lote foi produzido por veteranos da Primeira Guerra Mundial num hospital militar de Toronto.

fontes.trecho: The Iron Ring is a ring worn by many Canadian engineers as a symbol and reminder of the obligations and ethics associated with their profession. [...] The concept of the ritual and the rings originated from H. E. T. Haultain in 1922, with assistance from Rudyard Kipling, who crafted the ritual at Haultain's request. [...] The text of the calling was written by English poet Rudyard Kipling, at the request of Haultain. [...] A myth persists that the initial batch of Iron Rings was made from the beams of the first Quebec Bridge, a bridge that collapsed during construction in 1907 due to poor planning and design by the overseeing engineers. However, the initial batch of Iron Rings were actually produced by World War I veterans at Christie Street Military Hospital in Toronto. [...] It is intended to be worn on the little finger of the working (dominant) hand. There, the facets act as a sharp reminder of one's obligation while the engineer works, because it could drag on the writing surface while the engineer is drawing or writing. [...] All camps except Toronto have stopped conferring rings made of iron and have switched to stainless steel.

The project failed twice during its construction, in 1907 and 1916, at the cost of 88 lives and additional people injured. [...] However, preliminary calculations made early in the planning stages were never properly checked when the design was completed. All went well until the bridge was nearing completion in the summer of 1907, when the QBRC site engineering team under Norman McLure began noticing increasing distortions of key structural members already in place: the bridge’s dead load was proving too heavy, with its own weight being far in excess of its carrying capacity. McLure became increasingly concerned and wrote repeatedly to QBRC consulting engineer Theodore Cooper, who at first replied that the problems were minor. [...] Cooper agreed that the issue was serious, and promptly telegraphed to the Phoenix Bridge Company: "Add no more load to bridge till after due consideration of facts." [...] Cooper's message was not passed on to Quebec before it was too late. Near quitting time on the afternoon of 29 August, after four years of construction, the south arm and part of the central section of the bridge collapsed into the St. Lawrence River in 15 seconds. Of the 86 workers on the bridge that day, 75 were killed and the rest were injured, making it the world's worst bridge construction disaster. Of these victims, 33 (some sources say 35) were Mohawk steelworkers from the Kahnawake reserve near Montreal

gancho: A gerência da NASA estimava em 1 em 100 mil o risco de perder um ônibus espacial; os engenheiros, em cerca de 1 em 100. No fim do programa, foram dois desastres em 135 voos.
explicacao: O físico Richard Feynman fez parte da comissão que investigou o acidente do Challenger, em 1986. Numa audiência televisionada, ele apertou um pedaço do material dos anéis de vedação dos foguetes laterais num grampo, mergulhou tudo num copo de água gelada e mostrou que, frio, o material perdia a elasticidade. Nas entrevistas, achou erros conceituais na gerência. Em testes antigos, alguns desses anéis tinham sido queimados até um terço da espessura, e os gerentes registraram isso como prova de um "fator de segurança" de 3. Para Feynman, era o contrário: uma peça que trinca, mesmo sem romper, tem fator de segurança zero, porque está com defeito. No apêndice que escreveu para o relatório, ele anotou a enorme divergência: as estimativas iam de cerca de 1 em 100, vindas dos engenheiros, a 1 em 100 mil, vindas da gerência. Este último número equivaleria a lançar uma nave por dia durante 300 anos e perder só uma. Ele descobriu que 1 em 100 mil era o índice que se queria ter num veículo tripulado, e que as chances das peças tinham sido deduzidas de trás para a frente. Ao fim do programa, foram dois desastres em 135 voos, cerca de 1 em 68. A socióloga Diane Vaughan descreveu depois a "normalização do desvio": uma prática insegura passa a parecer normal quando não provoca catástrofe na hora. Feynman resumiu: para uma tecnologia dar certo, a realidade precisa vir antes das relações públicas, porque a natureza não se deixa enganar.

fontes.trecho: During a televised hearing, Feynman demonstrated how the O-rings became less resilient and subject to seal failures at low temperatures by compressing a sample of the material in a clamp and immersing it in a glass of ice water. [...] His interviews of NASA's high-ranking managers revealed startling misunderstandings of elementary concepts. One was the determination of a safety factor. In one example, early tests resulted in some of the booster rocket's O-rings burning a third of the way through. [...] NASA managers recorded this as demonstrating that the O-rings had a "safety factor" of 3. [...] If a 1,000-pound truck drove across the bridge and a crack appeared in a beam, even just a third of the way through a beam, the safety factor is now zero: The bridge is defective, there was no safety factor at all, even though the bridge did not actually collapse. [...] was struck by management's claim that the risk of catastrophic malfunction on the shuttle was 1 in 105, i.e., 1 in 100,000. [...] Feynman discovered that the 1 in 105 figure was stating what they claimed the failure rate ought to be, given that it was a crewed vehicle, and working backward to generate the failure rate of components. [...] The estimates range from roughly 1 in 100 to 1 in 100,000. The higher figures come from the working engineers, and the very low figures from management. [...] Since 1 part in 100,000 would imply that one could put a Shuttle up each day for 300 years expecting to lose only one [...] (At the time of retirement, the Shuttle suffered two catastrophic failures across 135 flights, a failure rate of 1 in 68.) [...] "For a successful technology," Feynman concluded, "reality must take precedence over public relations, for nature cannot be fooled."

Normalization of deviance, according to American sociologist Diane Vaughan, is the process in which deviance from correct or proper behavior or rule becomes culturally normalized. Vaughan defines the process where a clearly unsafe practice becomes considered normal if it does not immediately cause a catastrophe [...] The original example cited by Vaughan is the events leading to the Space Shuttle Challenger disaster in 1986

gancho: Em 1967, uma ponte nos EUA caiu por causa de uma trinca de 2,5 mm numa única barra. Só havia outras duas pontes de desenho parecido, e uma é a Hercílio Luz, em Florianópolis, que tinha o dobro de barras em cada elo.
explicacao: A Silver Bridge, de 1928, ligava Ohio e Virgínia Ocidental sobre o rio Ohio. Era uma ponte pênsil que pendia de correntes formadas por barras de olhal, e cada elo tinha só duas barras em paralelo, de um aço novo, com mais que o dobro da resistência dos aços da época. A força extra permitiu usar menos barras, mas tirou a redundância: se uma rompesse, a outra ficaria muito sobrecarregada. Em 15 de dezembro de 1967, no horário de pico, a ponte desabou e 46 pessoas morreram. A investigação achou a origem numa única barra: uma trinca formada pelo atrito e aumentada pela corrosão, com só 2,5 mm de profundidade, que fez a peça quebrar de forma frágil. Com a corrente partida, a ponte inteira veio abaixo, já que numa ponte pênsil todas as partes se equilibram. A trinca seria quase impossível de ver numa inspeção da época. A ponte irmã de St. Marys foi fechada na hora e demolida. A Hercílio Luz usava o mesmo aço, mas tinha quatro barras por elo e maior fator de segurança. Mesmo assim, a corrosão a levou a ser fechada de vez em 1991, e ela só foi reaberta em 2019, depois de uma longa restauração. O desastre levou os EUA a criar seu primeiro programa nacional de inspeção de pontes.

fontes.trecho: The Silver Bridge was an eyebar-chain suspension bridge built in 1928 that carried U.S. Route 35 over the Ohio River, connecting Point Pleasant, West Virginia, and Gallipolis, Ohio. [...] On December 15, 1967, the Silver Bridge collapsed amid heavy rush-hour traffic, resulting in the deaths of 46 people, two of whom were never found. [...] The eyebars in the Silver Bridge offered little to no redundancy, as each chain link consisted of just two eyebars in parallel. [...] These eyebars were made of a new, higher-strength steel (more than twice the tensile strength of other steels of that era), which meant fewer eyebars per link were needed to achieve the required strength to support the bridge [...] However, with only two eyebars per link, the failure of one of them would hugely increase the loading on the other [...] A small crack was formed through fretting wear at the bearing, and grew through internal corrosion, a problem known as stress corrosion cracking. The crack was only about 0.1 inches (2.5 mm) deep when the link failed, breaking in a brittle fashion. [...] A collapse of the entire structure was inevitable since all parts of a suspension bridge are in equilibrium with one another. [...] The technology used for inspection at the time was not capable of detecting such cracks. [...] There were only two bridges built to a similar design, one upstream at St. Marys, West Virginia, and the notably longer Hercílio Luz Bridge at Florianópolis, Brazil. The St. Marys bridge was immediately closed to traffic and was demolished by the state in 1971. [...] Although both it and the Silver Bridge used the same type of high-strength steel for the eyebars, it was built to a higher safety factor than the West Virginia bridge and had greater redundancy, with each suspension chain using an array of four eyebars per link, compared to just two per link for the Silver Bridge. However, in 1991, the Florianópolis bridge was closed due to high levels of corrosion. Following extensive renovation, it reopened in December 2019. [...] its collapse ultimately led to the creation of the first national bridge inspection program in the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1968.

gancho: A ponte ferroviária do Tay, na Escócia, caiu numa tempestade em 1879 com um trem em cima. Seu projetista não previu nenhuma folga especial para o vento, em parte por um conselho do Astrônomo Real.
explicacao: A ponte, projetada por Thomas Bouch, tinha pilares de ferro mais estreitos e menos contraventados que outros projetos dele. Na noite de 28 de dezembro de 1879, durante um temporal, ela desabou quando um trem de passageiros a atravessava, e não houve sobreviventes. Anos antes, para um projeto de ponte pênsil sobre o estuário do Forth, Bouch tinha consultado o Astrônomo Real, George Biddell Airy. Airy disse que o vento podia chegar a 40 libras por pé quadrado em pontos isolados, mas que, num vão longo, 10 libras seriam uma média razoável. Guiado por isso, Bouch não fez nenhuma previsão especial de carga de vento na ponte do Tay. O inquérito concluiu que ela fora mal projetada, mal construída e mal mantida, e responsabilizou Bouch, que morreu menos de um ano depois, com a reputação arruinada. Daí em diante, as pontes britânicas tiveram de suportar vento lateral de 56 libras por pé quadrado. O projeto de Bouch para o Forth foi abandonado, e a ponte que acabou erguida ali, com outro desenho, foi inaugurada em 1890. A tragédia também inspirou um poema de William McGonagall, tido como tão ruim que chega a ser cômico.

fontes.trecho: The Tay Bridge disaster occurred during a violent European windstorm on Sunday 28 December 1879, when the first Tay Rail Bridge collapsed as a North British Railway (NBR) passenger train on the Edinburgh to Aberdeen Line travelling from Burntisland to Dundee passed over it, killing all aboard. The bridge, designed by Sir Thomas Bouch, used lattice girders supported by iron piers, with cast iron columns and wrought iron cross-bracing. The piers were narrower and their cross-bracing was less extensive and robust than on previous similar designs by Bouch. Bouch had sought expert advice on wind loading when designing a proposed rail bridge over the Firth of Forth; as a result of that advice he had made no explicit allowance for wind loading in the design of the Tay Bridge. [...] Bouch died less than a year after the disaster, his reputation ruined. Future British bridge designs had to allow for wind loadings of up to 56 pounds per square foot (2.7 kilopascals). Bouch's design for the Forth Bridge was not used. [...] Bouch said that whilst 20 psf (0.96 kPa) had been discussed, he had been "guided by the report on the Forth Bridge" to assume 10 psf (0.5 kPa) and therefore made no special allowance for wind loading. He was referring to advice given by the Astronomer Royal, Sir George Biddell Airy in 1873 when consulted about Bouch's design for a suspension bridge across the Firth of Forth; that wind pressures as high as 40 psf (2 kPa) might be encountered very locally, but averaged over a 1,600 ft (490 m) span 10 psf (0.5 kPa) would be a reasonable allowance. [...] There were no survivors [...] most famously William McGonagall's "The Tay Bridge Disaster", widely considered to be of such a low quality as to be comical.

The public inquiry into the disaster, chaired by Henry Cadogan Rothery, found the Tay Bridge to be "badly designed, badly constructed and badly maintained", with Bouch being "mainly to blame" for the defects in construction and maintenance and "entirely responsible" for the defects in design. [...] The bridge was opened on 4 March 1890 by the Duke of Rothesay

gancho: Em 1991, a base de concreto de uma plataforma de gás norueguesa afundou num fiorde durante a obra e, ao bater no fundo, provocou um tremor de magnitude 3. A causa principal foi um erro numa simulação de computador.
explicacao: A Sleipner A era uma plataforma do tipo Condeep, com uma base de câmaras de concreto que serviam de lastro e flutuação. Para encaixar o convés, a base era rebaixada aos poucos no fiorde de Gands, num ritmo de um metro a cada 20 minutos. Ao chegar a 65 metros, ouviram-se estrondos e o barulho de água entrando: uma parede de uma das câmaras tinha cedido. A água entrou mais rápido do que as bombas davam conta, e em poucos minutos a estrutura afundava um metro por minuto. Enquanto ela descia no fiorde, de 210 metros, as câmaras de flutuação implodiram, e o choque dos destroços contra o fundo causou o tremor. Ninguém se feriu. A investigação do instituto norueguês SINTEF achou a causa num cálculo por elementos finitos: as tensões nas câmaras tinham sido subestimadas em 47%, e algumas paredes ficaram finas demais para a pressão da água. Pesquisadores da Universidade de Toronto, contratados pela firma projetista, concluíram que a parede que cedeu não tinha armadura transversal porque a análise global subestimou muito o cisalhamento nas pontas dela; o modelo deles previu a ruptura aos 62 metros. A base foi redesenhada, a plataforma ficou pronta em junho de 1993, e o caso virou lição para engenheiros que trabalham com simulações numéricas.

fontes.trecho: It is known for its catastrophic failure during construction on 23 August 1991, due to a design flaw, that resulted from an error caused by unconservative concrete codes and inaccurate finite element analysis modelling of the tricell, which formed part of the ballasting/flotation system. [...] It was towed into Gandsfjord where it was to be lowered in the water in a controlled ballasting operation at a rate of 1 meter per 20 minutes. [...] As the hull was lowered to the 65-meter (213 ft) mark, rumbling noises were heard followed by the sound of water pouring into the unit. A cell wall had failed and a serious crack had developed, and sea water poured in at a rate that was too great for the deballasting pumps to deal with. Within a few minutes the hull began sinking at a rate of 1 meter per minute. As the structure sank deeper into the 210-meter (690 ft) fjord, the buoyancy chambers imploded and the rubble struck the floor of the fjord, creating a Richter magnitude scale 3 earthquake. Later analysis showed that the failure would occur at 62 meters (203 feet). No one was injured during the accident. [...] The post-accident investigation by SINTEF in Norway discovered that the root cause of the failure resulted from inaccurate NASTRAN calculations in the design of the structure. Stresses on the ballast chambers were underestimated by 47% and some concrete walls were designed too thin to resist foreseeable hydrostatic pressure when submerged. [...] provide extremely valuable lessons for practising engineers working with numerical simulation tools such as the finite element method. [...] The hull was redesigned after the accident and the Sleipner A Platform was successfully completed in June 1993.

fontes.titulo: Failure of an offshore platform (Canadian Consulting Engineer)
fontes.trecho: Professors Michael P. Collins and Frank J. Vecchio of the University of Toronto were retained by Dr. techn.Olav Olsen a.s., the Norwegian structural engineering firm responsible for the design, to develop a better understanding of the factors influencing the failure of the tricell wall. [...] The first computer run on the Sleipner analytical model predicted that the as-built structure would fail when the applied water pressure on the inner faces of the tricell reached a head of 62 metres [...] The tricell wall that failed did not contain stirrups because the global finite element analysis performed as part of the design seriously underestimated the magnitude of the shear at the ends of the wall

gancho: Em 2012, uma corretora dos EUA perdeu mais de 460 milhões de dólares por 45 minutos de ordens descontroladas: uma função antiga, fora de uso mas nunca apagada, voltou a funcionar. E-mails automáticos tinham avisado.
explicacao: A Knight Capital era a maior negociadora de ações dos EUA, com algoritmos de alta frequência. Em 2005, a empresa mudou de lugar um trecho de código no seu roteador automático de ordens, o que deixou defeituosa uma função antiga, chamada Power Peg. Embora ela não devesse mais ser usada, a empresa a deixou lá. Em julho de 2012, ao preparar o sistema para um novo programa da Bolsa de Nova York, um técnico esqueceu de copiar o código novo para um dos oito servidores. O código novo reaproveitava um sinalizador que antes ligava a Power Peg, e as ordens que chegavam a esse servidor acordaram a função velha, que não reconhecia quando um pedido já tinha sido atendido. Em 1º de agosto, nos primeiros 45 minutos do pregão, o sistema disparou mais de 4 milhões de ordens tentando cumprir só 212 pedidos de clientes e negociou mais de 397 milhões de ações, acumulando posições de bilhões de dólares que, ao serem desfeitas, deram o prejuízo de mais de 460 milhões. Antes da abertura, um sistema interno já tinha enviado 97 e-mails a funcionários apontando um erro no roteador, mas eles não eram alertas formais e ninguém agiu. As ações da empresa despencaram, ela precisou de um resgate e acabou comprada meses depois. A SEC, órgão regulador do mercado, multou a corretora em 12 milhões de dólares.

fontes.titulo: SEC Charges Knight Capital With Violations of Market Access Rule (SEC, 16 out. 2013)
fontes.trecho: Knight Capital Americas LLC has agreed to pay $12 million to settle charges that it violated the agency’s market access rule in connection with the firm’s Aug. 1, 2012 trading incident that disrupted the markets. [...] Knight Capital moved a section of computer code in 2005 to an earlier point in the code sequence in an automated equity router, rendering a function of the router defective. Although this function was not meant to be used, Knight left it in the router. In late July 2012 when preparing for participation in the NYSE’s new Retail Liquidity Program, Knight Capital incorrectly deployed new code in the same router. As a result, certain orders eligible for the NYSE’s program triggered the defective function in Knight Capital’s router, which was then unable to recognize when orders had been filled. During the first 45 minutes after the market opened on August 1, Knight Capital’s router rapidly sent more than 4 million orders into the market when attempting to fill just 212 customer orders. Knight Capital traded more than 397 million shares, acquired several billion dollars in unwanted positions, and eventually suffered a loss of more than $460 million. The SEC’s order also finds that an internal Knight Capital system generated 97 automated emails that went to a group of personnel. The emails referenced the router and identified an error before the markets opened on August 1. [...] Although Knight Capital did not design these messages to be system alerts, they provided an opportunity to identify and fix the problem before the markets opened.

With its high-frequency trading algorithms Knight was the largest trader in U.S. equities [...] The company agreed to be acquired by Getco LLC in December 2012 after an August 2012 trading error lost $460 million. [...] The incident happened after a technician forgot to copy the new Retail Liquidity Program (RLP) code to one of the eight SMARS computer servers, which was Knight's automated routing system for equity orders. RLP code repurposed a flag that was formerly used to activate an old function known as 'Power Peg'. Orders sent with the repurposed flag to the eighth server triggered the defective Power Peg code still present on that server. [...] This caused Knight Capital's stock price to collapse [...] On August 5, the company raised around $400 million from half a dozen investors led by Jefferies in an attempt to stay in business after the trading error.
